title: University libraries between cost-cutting measures and open access transformation
content: From Google's English:  “When considering the financial resources of university libraries, two fundamental developments must be distinguished, both of which impact their budgets,” explains André Karliczek, Deputy Director of the Thuringian University and State Library Jena (ThULB). “Firstly, these libraries, whose core mission is providing information for study, research, and teaching, are increasingly becoming the primary bearers of publication costs in the course of the open access transformation – particularly within the framework of the DEAL agreements – because publishers have shifted their business model from subscription to open access publication. Acquisition budgets are therefore no longer solely used to purchase and license literature, but increasingly also to finance publication fees. Secondly, the changed economic conditions imposed by the federal and state governments necessitate the management of reduced expenditures – though to very different degrees depending on the specific area of ​​responsibility and the federal state.”

title: Beyond metric reductionism: assessment creep as an emerging risk of research evaluation reform | Research Evaluation | Oxford Academic
content: Abstract:  Recent research assessment reforms have successfully challenged the overreliance on simplistic quantitative indicators and promoted broader approaches to evaluation. This paper argues that these reforms may also generate a new risk: assessment creep, understood as the gradual accumulation of evaluation criteria without sufficient attention to how they are prioritised and combined. While criteria such as open science, societal impact, international collaboration, leadership, and mentoring may each be valuable, their proliferation can reduce transparency and make evaluation systems more difficult to understand and scrutinise. Less transparent systems may also make it harder to distinguish legitimate expert judgement from arbitrary decision-making and to detect favouritism or other forms of unwarranted advantage. Drawing on recent debates surrounding responsible research assessment, the paper suggests that the next challenge is not choosing between metrics and expert judgement, but designing evaluation systems that remain coherent, transparent, and accountable as they become increasingly complex.

title: TOP 2025: An update to the Transparency and Openness Promotion Guidelines - PhilPapers
content: Abstract: BackgroundTransparency and openness are core scientific values that enable independent verification of reported research results. The Transparency and Openness Promotion (TOP) Guidelines, first published in 2015 (TOP 2015), provided a flexible framework for journals to design and implement publication standards promoting these values. Over the past decade, widespread use of TOP 2015 contributed to valuable evidence and feedback for refinement.Main TextThe TOP Advisory Board undertook a comprehensive update of TOP 2015 that went into effect in 2025 (TOP 2025). The update introduces an explicit conceptual framework clarifying its primary objective: improving the verifiability of empirical research claims. Standards are reorganized into three categories (Research Practices, Verification Practices, and Verification Studies) that resolve conceptual and structural limitations of TOP 2015. Research Practices include seven discrete practices implemented in three ways: Disclosed, Shared and Cited, and Certified. title: How a Diamond Open Access Publisher Expanded into Open Textbooks - Pressbooks
content:
The University of Groningen Press (UGP) is a Diamond Open Access university press based in the Netherlands and a member of the Netherlands University Presses (NUPs) network. Since its founding in 2017, the press has supported the publication of Diamond Open Access scholarly journals and books.

In 2021, UGP expanded into a closely related—but distinct—area of open publishing by launching an open textbook pilot. As part of the University’s broader commitment to open education and open science, the initiative explored how UGP could apply its scholarly publishing expertise and open infrastructure to help faculty create high-quality open textbooks and other open educational resources.

What began as a pilot has since developed into an institutional service supporting multiple models of textbook production, enabling collaboration across institutions, and supporting the creation of interactive learning materials designed for teaching and learning contexts.

title: Panel: Hoe maken we Open Science echt gelijkwaardig?
content: How can science and knowledge production become more open, inclusive and equitable? This is not only a question of access to existing knowledge, but also of agency: who formulates research questions, who is recognised as a knowledge producer, and which forms of knowledge are considered legitimate? During the Netherlands National Open Science Week, Leiden University’s three UNESCO Chairs will come together to discuss these questions. The Chairs maintain broad international networks and collaborate with researchers and knowledge communities in Africa, Asia and Latin America. Their work covers diversity in science, digital diversity, colonial history, and collaboration with societal and international knowledge communities. The central question of the panel is how researchers, universities and research funders can contribute to more equitable international collaboration. The panellists will also critically examine the distribution of resources, authorship, theoretical authority and institutional recognition. content: Abstract: Introduction: Technological advancements and the intensification of information production pose new challenges for information management, requiring tools capable of organizing, preserving, and disseminating knowledge in digital environments. title: Risks and possibilities in sharing preprints during the doctorate - University of Southern Denmark
content: Abstract:  During doctoral candidature, students may seek to publish journal articles, which they may incorporate in their thesis if their institutional policy permits. They may consider sharing pre-prints of these texts either pre- or post-publication to promote open access and knowledge mobilisation. There is very little extant research that explores doctoral students’ knowledge of the risks and possibilities involved in sharing their work in this form, and this chapter seeks to identify those that they could encounter. It offers immediate value for informing doctoral education and a useful foundation for future research that is specific to the doctoral student experience.

content: "This study examined the adoption of Open Access (OA) publishing among librarians and Library and Information Science (LIS) educators in federal universities in North-Central Nigeria, with particular attention to the moderating roles of publishing behaviour and research assessment practices. A systematic review design was adopted to synthesise empirical and theoretical literature published between 2020 and 2026. Relevant sources were retrieved from Google Scholar, Web of Science, and the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ), and the extracted data were analysed using thematic content analysis guided by the PRISMA protocol. Findings showed that the level of OA adoption among librarians and LIS educators is moderate but increasing, driven by awareness of visibility, accessibility, and global dissemination benefits associated with open scholarship. content: Abstract: The shift from closed scholarship to open science has sparked the importance of Research Data Management (RDM) in supporting Open Access (OA) in academic institutions. While RDM has received significant attention in developed countries, its implementation in many developing contexts, including South African universities, remains uneven despite the existence of institutional policies and open science initiatives. This paper explores the perceptions of academic librarians on RDM practices for promoting OA in South African universities. The study was underpinned by constructs from the Digital Curation Centre (DCC) Lifecycle Model to understand RDM practices. Through an interpretive paradigm, utilising a qualitative research approach purposively selected librarians responsible RDM services provided their perceptions on using RDM as a tool to support OA in their libraries. title: The Crisis of Scholarly Communication in the Open Access Environment: Pathways to Diamond Open Access[v1] | Preprints.org
content: Abstract: This paper presents a critical analysis of the current system of scholarly communication, which has undergone a profound transformation under the influence of excessive commercialization within the neoliberal "publish or perish" paradigm. The study demonstrates that the Open Access movement, in its current form, has been co-opted by major commercial publishers through mechanisms such as Article Processing Charges (APCs) and "Transformative Agreements," which fail to solve the problem of creating a fair and accessible environment for the dissemination of knowledge. The work substantiates the thesis that the prestige of academic journals has ceased to be a reliable indicator of scientific quality, and that the traditional peer-review system is in a state of crisis, driven by the exponential growth of publications and a catastrophic shortage of qualified reviewers. The author analyzes potential solutions to this impasse, including a transition to platform-based publication and review models, as well as the advancement of Diamond Open Access. title: Who Owns Discovery? Academic Capitalism, Prestige Markets, and the Enclosure of Science
content: Abstract: Academic publishing rests on an institutional paradox that borders on the absurd. Public institutions finance much of the research and universities pay the scientists; those scientists then write the papers and typically supply peer review without compensation from publishers, while publishers often acquire exclusive rights and sell access back to the institutions that provided both the knowledge and the evaluative labor. Smaller universities and peripheral research systems contribute to a global scholarly record that their libraries may struggle to afford, while their researchers face a second barrier when publication itself carries a fee. This article reconstructs how that arrangement emerged through the history of publishing, the sociology of science, industrial organization, research evaluation, open access, and the political economy of artificial intelligence. Necessary infrastructure becomes a source of rent when exclusive rights, non-substitutable catalogues, and brands used to allocate jobs and funding are integrated with data and platforms. title: Choosing What’s Next: Introducing the National Open Education Priorities Process — Open Education Association
content: "Open education is more relevant to the problems facing higher education than ever before, yet it is too often absent from the rooms where decisions are made. Twenty years of OER advocacy successfully made the case against expensive textbooks. That case still holds, but it no longer opens every door it used to. This fall, the Open Education Association invites the open education field to collaborate on a process to choose national priorities: specific problems that higher education leaders and policymakers are already trying to solve, where open education offers a solution. Examples could include how to train nurses faster by reducing cost as a barrier, how to break down silos in educational data, or how to improve AI literacy through open materials. Working collaboratively across the field, this process will surface a list of potential priorities, discuss them throughout the fall, and select the final priorities at a national summit in November. title: NOT-OD-26-100: Implementation Update: NIH Data Management and Sharing Plan Requirements
content: "This Guide Notice provides an update to the research community on forms changes when NIH transitions to the updated Data Management and Sharing (DMS) Plan format which includes reporting changes to previously approved DMS Plans. Background The NIH Data Management and Sharing (DMS) Policy ensures that the benefits of taxpayer funded research are maximally shared to advance research, improve health outcomes, and cultivate trust in the biomedical research enterprise. When released in 2023, NIH issued supplemental information outlining desired elements of a DMS Plan. After several years of implementation experience, NIH issued Notice NOT-OD-26-046, Updated Elements of an NIH Data Management and Sharing Plan, to provide a structured template and format across all NIH Institutes, Centers, and Offices (ICOs.) NIH is finalizing implementation of this new format to ensure NIH's data sharing goals are achieved while reducing administrative burden and improving reporting efficiency. title: Examining Persistence of European Open Repository Infrastructure and its Diffusion in the Scholarly Record | International Journal of Digital Curation
content: Abstract: This article seeks to determine the extent to which the principle of persistence is observed by repositories and the organizations that operate them. In addition, the impact that negative repository persistence levels may be having on the scholarly record is assessed. This is achieved by interrogating and combining data on European repositories from several repository registries and web-scraped sources, including the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine, which creates a unique dataset of historic repository locations and their OAI-PMH endpoints. Then, this data is used as the basis for text mining CORE, a vast corpus of scholarly outputs, to determine the extent to which impersistent European repository content has permeated the scholarly literature. The findings indicate that over one-fifth of European repositories (greater than 20 per cent) could be classified as “dead,” with an even greater proportion (greater than 40 per cent) of the machine interfaces associated with these repositories similarly dead. title: [2607.00546v1] Open Science in Astrophysics: Citation Benefits of Open Code, Open Data, and Open Access
content: Abstract: We analyze the relationship between open-accessibility in data, code, and paper text in astrophysics using a sample of 53,194 peer reviewed papers published between January 2021 and April 2025, drawn from NASA's Astrophysics Data System (ADS). We measure eleven quantities: open accessibility of text, open-code status, open-data status, number of grants received, code size, programming language, data repository size, citation count, number of authors, paper length, and publication date. We break down citation advantages based on six astrophysical sub-fields: Solar System, Planet, Stellar, ISM, High Energy, and Galaxies+Cosmology, determined by keywords. This is accomplished by tuning a multivariate least-squares regression model with alongside partial correlations and non-parametric tests to isolate the contribution of each facet of openness. After controlling for the aforementioned quantities, we find significant citation advantages associated with all three forms of openness: open data (+32%, p < 10^-24), open access (+26%, p < 10^-67), and open code (+16%, p = 0.003). The open-data citation advantage is present in all six sub-fields, and especially in Galaxies+Cosmology

title: Community Peer Review for Resistance and Resilience
content: "Scholarly communication benefits from multiple pathways for evaluating research rather than relying exclusively on traditional journal-organized peer review. Across the open science ecosystem, organizations are experimenting with ways to separate the functions of publishing, reviewing, and curating research, broadening participation while reducing dependence on any single institution or gatekeeper. This broader vision is reflected in the growing Publish–Review–Curate (PRC) movement. PREreview is one example within this ecosystem. Our focus is on building open tools and cultivating communities that connect researchers seeking feedback with people willing to share their expertise. Other organizations are exploring complementary approaches. Review Commons coordinates expert peer review independently of journals before manuscript submission, allowing reviews to travel with the work across participating publishers. title: How collective funding supports sustainable publishing
content:
"Diamond open access is defined by UNESCO as ‘an equitable scholarly publishing model, supported by shared infrastructures and open licensing, providing scholarly knowledge as a digital public good with no fees for readers or authors.’ One increasingly important approach to funding this form of open access is collective funding, which allows libraries to directly support publishers and publishing infrastructure, making it possible to publish without the need for article or book publication charges. 

As members of initiatives such as the Open Book Collective (OBC) and Open Journals Collective (OJC), who have both recently signed a Memorandum of Understanding, and with a Jisc-supported scheme for our journals programme, LSE Press is part of this wider movement that seeks to establish more equitable, sustainable, community-governed alternatives for open access publishing. Together, OBC and Jisc membership has already brought us support from 29 libraries across the UK, Europe and North America."

title: Coalition for Resilient Research Data Infrastructure (CRRDI): A Community-Driven Strategic Plan, 2027 – 2030 | Zenodo
content: Abstract: Federally funded research data is a public good, but the repositories and infrastructure that keep it findable, accessible, and usable have long been fragile — a fragility that recent funding, staffing, and policy disruptions have laid bare. Because the research data system is highly distributed, spanning thousands of repositories and practitioners across many domains, no single organization can address these vulnerabilities alone. This document is the draft strategic plan for the Coalition for Resilient Research Data Infrastructure (CRRDI), a proposed cross-sectoral coalition working to build a more resilient ecosystem for federally funded research data. It sets out the case for action, a shared vision and guiding principles, and three strategic pillars: assessing and monitoring the repository landscape; developing diverse, sustained funding and governance; and building a shared outreach, advocacy, and action strategy. It also includes a starting point for coalition governance and an outline of next steps toward implementation. title: How preprints accelerate the time to first citation of the subsequent journal articles? | Scientometrics | Springer Nature Link
content: Abstract: This study examines whether journal articles with preprints are cited more rapidly than those without preprints. We construct a matched sample of articles published in the same journal, year, volume, and issue to ensure comparability between articles with and without preprints. Survival analysis is employed to estimate the temporal advantage of articles with preprints in receiving the first citation relative to those without preprints, while OLS regression quantifies this advantage in terms of days. The key findings are as follows: (1) articles with preprints have a 35.2% higher hazard of receiving their first citation than those without preprints; (2) among articles that received at least one citation during the observation period, articles with preprints were associated with a 69.042-day shorter time to first citation than comparable articles without preprints; (3) both early visibility and the additional dissemination channels of preprint platforms are associated with a shorter time to first citation, with early visibility showing a relatively stronger association. title: Utilization of Institutional Repositories among Users in Selected Universities in Karnataka: An Empirical Study
content: Abstract: The present study examines the utilization of Institutional Repositories among users in selected universities in Karnataka. The study is based on primary data collected through a structured questionnaire from teaching faculty and research scholars. The findings revealed that a large proportion of respondents (87.16%) were aware of Institutional Repositories, and a majority (75.31%) actively used them for academic and research purposes. Institutional Repositories were primarily utilized for accessing research-related materials and supporting scholarly activities. The study further indicated that users perceived several benefits, including enhanced accessibility and visibility of scholarly work, increased citation impact, and long-term preservation of institutional outputs. However, respondents also reported challenges such as technical issues, poor browsing ability, limited access to repository resources, and lack of institutional support, which affected effective utilization. title: [2607.25220v1] Preprints Without Curation Are Increasingly Cited by Journals
content: Abstract: The recent strain on peer review systems necessitates the publish-review-curate model, where the public dissemination of manuscripts is decoupled from formal peer review and later editorial processes. Citation norms traditionally pointed to the curated version; those that subsequently appear in peer-reviewed journals. Citations to preprints are therefore generally expected to occur only to those eventually curated. Using metadata from six major preprint servers linked to the world's largest bibliographic reference database, and focusing on citations from long-established journals with rigorous editorial workflows, we compare observed citation rates with a null model reflecting the expected rate if authors were indifferent between preprints and journal articles. The growth is evident in both citation intensity and the breadth of adoption: at its peak in 2021, nearly one in five journal articles cited at least one preprint. The preference to cite preprints has grown exponentially since the mid-2010s, with key inflection points coinciding with the launch of bioRxiv (2013) and the introduction of a preprint content type in Crossref's DOI system (2016). title: Openness and Inequity in Scientific Research
content: "This special issue examines the promises and limitations of Open Science (OS) and the conditions that produce inequity, injustice, and exclusion in research. Going well beyond the free sharing of publications typically referred to as Open Access, OS aspires to take advantage of new communication technologies to enhance access to and use of all the components of research, ranging from data to models, software, techniques, instruments, protocols and review procedures (Boulton and Royal Society Citation2012). OS advocates argue that the competitive and proprietary regimes and metrics under which research is currently conducted damage the reliability, quality, and social relevance of science. The main reason is that these regimes and metrics erode opportunities for critical scrutiny and collaboration which are the hallmarks of scientific work. They also disincentivise the exchange of insights and methods within and across disciplines (Radder Citation2010) leading to an inward-looking academic culture more interested in competing for the next high-impact publication than in developing reliable long-term solutions to societal and environmental challenges (Edwards and Roy Citation2017).

title: The Diamond road to Open Science | Swiss Medical Weekly
content: Abstract: Diamond Open Access is the fairest and most sustainable model for scientific communication. The Diamond model promotes editorial independence, supports researchers by waiving article processing charges, and serves as an indispensable public research infrastructure. “Read & Publish” agreements increase dependence on large commercial publishers, and some of the funds currently spent on such agreements could instead be used to provide long-term support for Diamond journals. Promising models for sustainable funding and collaboration are emerging through national and international initiatives. However, Switzerland is already providing concrete evidence that institutions do not have to wait until national mechanisms are fully developed. In 2025, the University of Lausanne launched the “Diamond Open Access Fund”, a pioneering initiative of its kind in Switzerland. The future development of Diamond Open Access should focus not only on sustainable funding but also on enhancing the quality, transparency, and culture of scholarly publishing. title: “We publish open access as outsiders”: a Bourdieuan approach to understanding marginalised academics’ publishing community | Journal of Professional Capital and Community | Emerald Publishing
content: Abstract: Purpose The purpose of this study is to explore the motivations and experiences of university academics who engage in open access publishing for survival and academic development. Design/methodology/approach This study employs a multiple-case qualitative approach, drawing on Bourdieu’s theory of practice to investigate the activities and experiences of seven academics as they strived to publish in indexed open access journals. Data were collected through in-depth interviews and observation, focusing on the academics’ strategies for obtaining cultural capital. Findings Findings reveal that they viewed this publishing community more as an imagined or virtual community from which they could obtain cultural capital and seek the sense of belonging to compensate for the outsider identity and peripheral positioning within their institutions.
